open-question.question: When the fold tool's replace mode is given a `--section` heading that matches no `###` subsection under `## Decisions`, does it refuse with one `Error:` line and leave the file unchanged, or create the subsection at the end of the section as `fold` does?
open-question.recommendation: A replace exists to rewrite an entry that already stands, so an unmatched heading is always a mistyped or misaimed call; refusing turns it into the sweep's resumable stop, where creating would leave the superseded entry standing beside a new subsection, the very outcome the replace exists to remove.
open-question.alternative: The replace mode matches `--section` against the `###` headings under `## Decisions` with the same whitespace- and case-folded exact equality `fold` uses. When no subsection matches, it prints one `Error:` line on stderr naming the heading, exits 1, and leaves `requirements.md` byte-for-byte unchanged. It never creates a subsection, so a replace can only rewrite an entry that already exists. `fold` keeps its create-at-end behaviour. A replace exists to rewrite an entry that is already standing, so a heading matching nothing is always a mistake: a mistyped heading, or the runner pointing at the wrong pair. Refusing turns that mistake into a visible stop. The sweep's batched call already treats a fold refusal as a resumable `stopped at` with the tree left as it was. Creating instead would leave the superseded entry standing beside a new subsection, which is the both-entries-standing outcome this milestone sets out to remove. The reason `fold` creates a missing heading (so one call shape can serve a fresh milestone's first decision) has no counterpart here, because there is never a first entry to replace. Every refusal stops the sweep's batched call. A near-miss heading that a human would read as the intended subsection halts the whole run at that question until someone corrects the heading and re-runs. The tool's two writing modes also handle the same input differently, which adds one refusal case to the tests and one more case for the runtime prose to keep apart from `fold`'s create rule.

When `--section` matches no `###` subsection, the replace mode behaves exactly as `fold` does on a missing heading. It creates the subsection at the end of `## Decisions` and writes the stdin body under it. Nothing is refused and nothing existing is rewritten. On an unmatched heading, a replace is indistinguishable from a fold, and the writes are a success. The two modes share one rule for an unmatched heading, so the tool has no new refusal case and the sweep's conflict-question section can never stop on a heading. The batched call keeps the property that a well-formed decision always lands, and any near-duplicate subsection the creation produces shows in that answer's commit diff and stays revertable. A wrong or mistyped heading fails silently. The losing entry stays standing unchanged and the new text lands under a fresh subsection, so the conflict the question was meant to settle is recorded as two standing entries again, with no stop and no `Error:` line. The milestone's goal is to rewrite superseded entries instead of appending beside them, and this outcome is exactly what that goal targets. The only remaining catch is a later review pass's consistency step noticing the pair again.

The replace mode takes an optional flag (named, for example, `--create`). Without the flag, an unmatched heading is refused with one `Error:` line and the file left unchanged. With the flag, an unmatched heading creates the subsection at the end of `## Decisions` as `fold` does. Each call decides, so the caller chooses per invocation whether a missing subsection is an error or a place to write. Both behaviours are available. The default guards against a mistyped heading silently leaving a superseded entry standing, and a caller that knows the heading is new can still write the rewrite without switching to `fold`. Only the sweep calls the tool, and its batched call has one fixed section shape with no branch per question kind. Using the flag on some questions and not others would bring in exactly the per-question judgment and call variation the fixed shape exists to rule out. Always passing it, or never passing it, collapses this option into one of the other two while still paying for an extra flag, its tests, and its one-sentence contract at the call site. If replace is a flag on `fold` rather than its own subcommand (the invocation question decides this), a second modifier flag on the same subcommand also complicates the argparse contract.

open-question.question: Is the `## Noted contradictions` section created empty with every milestone by the milestone-definition tool, so every `requirements.md` carries five sections and the four-section structure stated in `review-milestone-requirements` and `CLAUDE.md` changes, or created by the first single-question answer skill that writes a note and absent from a milestone that never records a conflict?
open-question.recommendation: No tool, template, or test changes, a milestone that never notes a conflict stays byte-for-byte as today, and the heading's presence alone means unresolved notes stand, which a finished milestone's file then shows without inspecting the section; the review pass already deletes notes under the goal, so removing an emptied heading is one more line of the same edit.
open-question.alternative: The milestone-definition tool and its template stay unchanged at four sections. The first note-writing step that records a conflict in a milestone inserts the `## Noted contradictions` heading together with its note; when the review pass turns the last standing note into an open question and deletes it, it deletes the heading too, so the section exists only while at least one note stands. The structure statements in `review-milestone-requirements` and `CLAUDE.md` keep the four sections and add one optional fifth, present only while a note stands. No tool, template, or test changes, a milestone that never records a conflict is byte-for-byte what it is today, and the heading's mere presence means "unresolved notes stand", so a reader (or a finished milestone's file) shows leftover notes without inspecting the section's body. Both writers take on a structural edit: the note writer must insert a heading at the right place and the review pass, which today states it does not edit `requirements.md`, must remove one in addition to the notes, and a missed removal leaves an empty heading that breaks the presence-means-pending reading. Where the heading is inserted depends on the position the sibling question on the section's position settles.

The milestone-definition tool's fixed template in `core/tools/define_milestone.py` gains an empty `## Noted contradictions` heading, so every milestone defined after this release carries five sections from creation; its docstring, `tests/test_define_output.py`, the four-section "document structure" block of `review-milestone-requirements`, and the milestone file structure in `CLAUDE.md` are restated as five sections. The note-writing step still creates the heading when it is absent, for milestones defined before the release (this milestone included, and in-flight milestones in projects already loading the plugin), since there is no migration. When the review pass deletes the last note it deletes only the entries, leaving the empty heading standing. For every newly defined milestone the note writer only appends under a heading that is always there, and the file's shape is one fixed structure that every reader and the structure statements describe without a condition, so the new section is visible as a standing place to look rather than something a reader must know may appear. It changes a tool, its docstring, and its output test, and edits every restatement of the structure, yet still leaves the note writer a create-if-absent path for older milestones, so two creation paths exist; and every milestone, most of which never record a conflict, carries an empty heading that whole-file readers such as `derive-tasks` and `finish-current-milestone` read past. Where the fallback inserts the heading depends on the position the sibling question on the section's position settles.

The milestone-definition tool and its template stay unchanged at four sections. The first note-writing step that records a conflict in a milestone inserts the `## Noted contradictions` heading together with its note; the review pass deletes the notes it turns into open questions and leaves the heading standing, so a milestone that has ever noted a conflict keeps the section, empty or not, and one that never has carries none. The structure statements in `review-milestone-requirements` and `CLAUDE.md` keep the four sections and add one optional fifth, created by the first note. No tool, template, or test changes, and each writer has the smallest rule: the note writer creates the heading only if absent, and the review pass removes only note entries, never touching the heading. The file's shape depends on its history, with three states (absent, present and empty, present with notes), so the empty heading carries no meaning and every structure statement must describe a section that may or may not be there. Where the heading is inserted depends on the position the sibling question on the section's position settles.

open-question.question: When a single-question answer skill records an answer to an ordinary question and finds it contradicts a standing `## Decisions` entry of another question, does it always write a note and leave the old entry as it stands, or does it rewrite the old entry when the answer plainly supersedes it and write a note only when the answer does not plainly settle which entry should hold?
open-question.recommendation: An answer that knowingly replaces an earlier decision is fixed in its own commit, with no review, question, and answer cycle holding `/derive-tasks`, while doubt notes, so only unsettled pairs reach the review pass; the goal already permits bending an entry to a recorded answer, and one commit per answer keeps a wrong rewrite one revert away.
open-question.alternative: The analyse step judges each contradiction it finds. When the new answer plainly supersedes the old entry, because the user's answer is clearly meant to replace it, the fold rewrites the conflicting text of that other question's entry in place in the same targeted edit pass, and writes no note. When the answer does not plainly settle which entry should hold, the old entry stays as written and a note is written. Doubt notes. The answer core's ban on otherwise rewriting `requirements.md` gains this one exception. The common case, an answer that knowingly replaces an earlier decision, is fixed in the same commit that records it, at no extra review, question, or answer cycle, and `requirements.md` never holds two contradicting sentences for that case. Only genuinely unsettled pairs reach the review pass, so noted contradictions stay rare and each one means a real open choice. One commit per answer still makes revert-then-re-answer restore the old entry. The supersession test is a runner judgment that can misfire, and a wrong rewrite silently edits a decision recorded under another question with nothing flagged. Only the commit diff shows it, and no question is held open for anyone to catch it. The rewritten lines also show up as added lines in that answer's `requirements.md` hunk, which `capture-milestone-principle-updates` reads as the recorded decision. Whether the recommendation skill makes the same judgment depends on which procedure carries the note step, which the note-writing-home sibling settles.

Every contradiction the analyse step finds against another question's standing `## Decisions` entry while recording an ordinary answer gets a note under `## Noted contradictions`, whether or not the answer plainly supersedes the old entry. The fold only appends the new decision, the old entry stays exactly as written, and the answer core's closing ban on otherwise rewriting `requirements.md` stays as it is for ordinary answers. An existing entry is rewritten only when a conflict question the review pass authored from the note is answered. Rewriting a decision recorded under another question always goes through one explicit, answerable conflict question, so no runner judgment of "plain supersession" ever silently changes an entry the user recorded earlier. The single-question fold keeps one rule with no judgment branch, and each answer commit's `requirements.md` diff stays exactly the folded decision plus at most a note. Every intended supersession, about 17 of the 38 pairs in the October 2 analysis, costs a review pass, a conflict question, its alternatives and recommendation, and another answer before the old entry is fixed, and the open conflict question blocks `/derive-tasks` in the meantime. It also forbids by rule what the Edit-based fold already does by runner judgment, as in the October 8 run that rewrote the superseded sentence during the fold.

When the analyse step judges that the answer plainly supersedes another question's standing entry, the inline skill asks the user once in the conversation whether to rewrite that entry. It rewrites the entry in place on a yes and writes a note on a no or when there is no reply. When the answer does not plainly settle which entry should hold, it writes a note without asking. A supersession is fixed in the answer's own commit, with no review cycle, only when a human has confirmed it, so no runner judgment alone ever rewrites another question's decision. Every refused or unanswered rewrite still lands in the note path. It adds a confirmation prompt to the single-question answer skills, which the workflow otherwise avoids so that headless chains have no prompt nobody is there to answer. In a headless run it falls back to always noting, so the same answer gets different handling depending on how the skill was invoked. Each runner also needs its own wording for asking and for treating no reply.

open-question.question: When the answer sweep's batched call records a conflict question whose answer rewrites entries under more than one `###` subsection, does that question's section carry one replace call per rewritten subsection chained ahead of its `remove`, or exactly one replace call for one subsection so every section keeps a fixed number of tool calls?
open-question.recommendation: The batched call keeps one fixed section shape per question kind, with replace standing where fold stands and no count for the runner to compose or the test to extract; the losing entry's subsection is the common supersession, and a stale clause under a second heading is left to the next review pass's consistency step, as mooted entries already are.
open-question.alternative: Every conflict question's section carries exactly one replace call for exactly one subsection, the one holding the losing entry, chained ahead of `remove`. The sweep never rewrites a second subsection. The winning entry and any knock-on clause elsewhere stay as written, and a residual conflict is left to the next review pass's `## Decisions` consistency step to flag as a new question. Every section of the batched call thus keeps a fixed number of tool calls, with the conflict section differing from an ordinary one only in replace standing where fold stands. The batched call keeps one fixed section shape with no count for the runner to judge or the test to extract. That matches the sweep's measured failure mode, where variable composition is what produced ad-hoc scripts, and it keeps a refused replace an all-or-nothing stop for its question. An answer that genuinely supersedes text under two headings is recorded only in part: the second stale entry stays in `requirements.md` until another review-and-answer round, which is the appended-beside-the-old-text residue this milestone exists to remove. Whether the winning heading also gets a statement depends on the conflict answer record question, a sibling's.

A conflict question's section carries one replace call for each `###` subsection the answer rewrites, as many as the decision needs, each its own `requirements.py` process on its own quoted heredoc, chained behind `&&` ahead of the section's `remove`. The rewrite scope is every entry the answer supersedes, including a clause correcting a third subsection that is not one of the two entries the question names. The section shape therefore varies: the shown call states the replace line as repeated once per rewritten subsection, and an ordinary question's section keeps its single fold. It is the only fixed-process-per-subsection shape that can fully remove superseded text wherever it sits. That covers the one recorded field case, where the sweep had to correct a clause living in a different subsection and could only append beside it, and it needs nothing from the tool beyond a single-subsection replace. The batched call loses its one fixed section shape: the runner composes a variable number of calls per conflict section, `tests/test_sweep_batched_call.py`'s extraction and the shown call need a repetition rule, and a refusal on the second replace leaves the first rewrite uncommitted for the stranded-fold guard to catch on the next run. How much one call rewrites depends on the replace mode's granularity, whole subsection body or one entry, which a sibling question owns.

A conflict question's section carries one replace call per subsection holding one of the two entries the question names, so one call when only the losing entry is rewritten or both sit under the same heading, and two when both named entries are rewritten under different headings. These are chained behind `&&` ahead of `remove`. Entries outside the named pair are never rewritten by the sweep, and any knock-on clause elsewhere is left standing for the next review pass's `## Decisions` consistency step. The count is bounded at two and follows from the question's own text, which names both headings, so the runner reads the call count off the question rather than judging how far the supersession reaches. That keeps the sweep close to its record-as-given stance while still allowing a reconciling answer that edits both entries. The section is still not one fixed shape (one or two replace calls), and the extraction test and shown call must show the optional second call. A supersession that reaches a third subsection survives the answer as a fresh conflict the next review pass has to re-author. Whether the winning entry is touched at all depends on how the conflict answer is recorded, which a sibling question owns.

A conflict question's section carries exactly one replace process that rewrites every subsection the answer supersedes in a single write. The replace mode takes the target headings and their new bodies together, for example a repeated `--section` with a delimited stdin, so the section's tool-call count stays fixed while the number of rewritten subsections varies. The tool resolves every named heading before it writes anything and refuses the whole replace, file unchanged, if any one fails. It keeps one fixed call per section and still lets a supersession reach every subsection it touches. One process makes the multi-subsection rewrite atomic, so no partial rewrite can be stranded, much as `remove` resolves every `--undermined` title before it changes anything. The fold tool gains a multi-target input format with its own delimiter, parsing, and tests, a larger surface than any other single-target tool call in the plugin. The runner still composes a variable-length heredoc whose structure must be right, so the composition risk moves into the stdin rather than disappearing. Its shape is conditioned on the replace mode's invocation and granularity, which sibling questions own.

Every conflict section the sweep writes carries exactly one replace call for the losing entry's subsection. A conflict question whose answer would rewrite more than one subsection gets no section in the batched call and is left standing for `answer-open-question-with-recommendation`, whose Edit-based fold can rewrite any number of entries by rule. The closing completeness `walk` then prints that id. The batched call keeps one fixed section shape, and the rare multi-subsection supersession is still recorded in full, on the path whose Edit-based fold already rewrites freely, so neither the tool nor the test grows for an edge case. It breaks the sweep's one-section-per-walked-question rule and its no-judgment stance: the runner must judge how far each conflict answer reaches before writing the call. The completeness `walk`'s print, now treated as an anomaly, would carry an expected id, so the report would need a new advisory naming the questions left for the single-question skill.

open-question.question: When a conflict question is answered and the losing entry is rewritten, is that rewrite the whole record of the decision, or is a decision statement also folded under the winning entry's heading, given that `capture-milestone-principle-updates` reads the recorded decision from the added lines of the answer commit's `requirements.md` hunk?
open-question.recommendation: The rewrite is the decision, so `## Decisions` ends the answer with one statement per point and no residue sentence, which is the milestone's aim; the commit body already carries the lifted option for capture, and a rewritten whole subsection body reads as a decision rather than a fragment.
open-question.alternative: The rewrite of the superseded entry (or entries) is the whole record of the conflict answer, in every runner: no separate decision statement is folded anywhere under `## Decisions`, the sweep's conflict section swaps its `fold` call for the replace call, and the single-question skills' Edit-based fold edits the losing entry in place and adds nothing. `capture-milestone-principle-updates` stays unchanged and takes the rewritten entry's added lines in the `requirements.md` hunk as the commit's recorded decision. The `## Decisions` section ends the answer holding exactly one statement per point, with no residue sentence saying which entry won, and the answer commit's `requirements.md` diff is just the rewrite, so the milestone's aim of replacing appended corrections is met in its purest form and the sweep's conflict section keeps the same number of writes as an ordinary one. Capture's recorded decision becomes the rewritten entry's new text, which states the surviving content in the losing entry's own subject rather than the choice made between the two entries, so a `Manual-answer:` whose body names no alternative id has weak text to match against alternatives phrased as "entry X stands", and when the losing entry's rewrite is small the added lines may be a fragment of a sentence that reads as no decision at all.

The rewrite is the whole record in every runner, as in rewrite-only, and no decision statement is folded; `capture-milestone-principle-updates` is extended so that for an answer commit whose `requirements.md` hunk holds removed `## Decisions` lines, it reads the removed and added lines together as a before/after pair and takes that pair, rather than the added lines alone, as the recorded decision. The record stays a single clean rewrite with no extra statement in the file, while capture sees exactly what changed and from what, which carries the choice between the two entries more faithfully than either the added lines alone or a separately composed summary. It widens the milestone into a skill the goal does not name, changing capture's per-commit reconstruction and its `recorded_decision` field for one class of commit, and the pair it reads is still raw diff lines whose meaning capture must reconstruct by reading, so the harvester gains a branch and a rule to keep in step with how rewrites are written.

In every runner the conflict answer both rewrites the superseded entry (or entries) and folds a concise decision statement, stating which content holds, under the `###` heading of the entry the answer keeps; where the answer keeps neither entry as written and rewrites both, the statement lands under the heading the question names first. The sweep's conflict section therefore carries the replace call or calls plus one `fold` ahead of its `remove`; capture stays unchanged and finds the statement among the hunk's added lines beside the rewrite. Capture's added lines always include a self-standing sentence stating the decision in the vocabulary of the question it answered, so the harvester needs no change and a `Manual-answer:` override has clear text to match against the alternatives, while the statement sits beside the content it confirms. The winning subsection gains a sentence that restates what its existing entry already says, which is the duplication and correction-style residue the milestone sets out to remove, and the sweep's conflict section carries one more tool call than its replace calls, whose number the call-count sibling settles; the both-rewritten case needs a fallback heading rule that can file the statement under a heading the answer did not favour.

In every runner the conflict answer rewrites the superseded entry (or entries) and folds a concise decision statement under a new `###` subsection of its own, its heading composed from the conflict question as any other answer's heading is, rather than under either conflicting entry's heading. The sweep's conflict section carries the replace call or calls plus its ordinary `fold`, now targeting that new heading; capture stays unchanged and reads the statement from the added lines. Capture gets a self-standing decision sentence with no change to the harvester, the sweep's conflict section keeps its ordinary `fold` with its usual heading rule so only the replace calls are added, and the statement needs no rule for which entry won, so it works the same whether the answer keeps one entry or rewrites both. Every answered conflict leaves a subsection in `## Decisions` that exists only to say the contradiction was settled, a meta-entry about two other entries that `/derive-tasks` and later reviews read as one more decision, and over a milestone with several conflicts these subsections accumulate as a provenance trail the rewrite was meant to make unnecessary.

The record differs by runner: the answer sweep rewrites only, its conflict section swapping `fold` for the replace call or calls so no statement is folded, while the three single-question answer skills both rewrite the losing entry and fold a decision statement placed by the answer core's existing fold rule, in a fitting existing subsection or a new one. Capture stays unchanged, reading a `Recommendation-answer:` commit's recorded decision from the rewrite's added lines and a `Manual-answer:` or `Alternative-answer:` commit's from the folded statement. The statement lands on exactly the commits capture treats as the signal for new principles, the hand answers that override a recommendation, while the sweep, whose accepted recommendations are evidence only and whose body already carries the lifted rationale, keeps a lean conflict section with no extra write. A conflict answer leaves two different shapes in `requirements.md` depending on which skill recorded it, a split every reader of the file and every later editor of the answer core and the sweep must keep in mind, and `answer-open-question-with-recommendation` and the sweep record the same pick in different shapes despite sharing the `Recommendation-answer:` subject.

open-question.question: Does the review pass author one open question for every entry under `## Noted contradictions` exactly as noted, or apply its own conflict test to each note first and delete a note it judges to be a refinement rather than a conflict without authoring a block?

recommendation.option: Clean up against recorded state only

open-question.recommendation: It applies to notes the rule the pass already applies to blocks, removing only what recorded state covers, an already-flagged pair or an entry since rewritten, so duplicate and moot questions are avoided while the answer skill's conflict verdict is never overruled on its merits and the pass stays on the tidy side.

alternative.id: Clean up against recorded state only

open-question.alternative: The review pass does not re-judge whether the pair conflicts. It checks each note only against what is already recorded. If a standing block already flags the pair, or if either named entry no longer stands as the note describes it (its heading is gone, or it has been rewritten so the two now hold together), the note is deleted with no block, as cleanup of recorded state. Every other note is authored as noted, one block per note, and then deleted. It applies to notes the same tidy-side rule the pass already uses for blocks: remove only what already-recorded state covers, an exact duplicate included. Duplicate and moot questions are avoided, while the answer skill's conflict verdict is never overruled on its merits. A note that was a refinement from the start, a false positive of the answer skill's analyse step, still becomes a question that holds task derivation for a full cycle. The check also needs the review pass to compare a note against the current entries, so its reliability depends on how precisely a note names its pair (the sibling question on note entry content) and on whether answers rewrite superseded entries in place (the sibling question on note versus rewrite at fold).

The review pass applies no test of its own to a note. Every entry under `## Noted contradictions` becomes exactly one block through step 3's `add`, its question built from the note's pair (the two `###` headings, what each entry says, which stands), and the note is then deleted. Not even a standing block that already flags the same pair, or a named entry that has since been rewritten, stops the authoring: the note is turned into a block exactly as written. The conflict judgment is made once, by the answer skill that saw the pair as it recorded the decision, and the review pass handles notes purely mechanically. A real conflict can never be lost to a second judgment that disagrees, and the review pass keeps its tidy-side role toward notes, with no reading of the note's merits. Every false positive and stale note costs a whole question cycle (alternatives, recommendation, answer) and holds `/derive-tasks`' precondition until that cycle is done. A pair that step 4's own scan already flagged, or one that a later answer has already settled, still produces a duplicate or moot block, which goes against the pass's existing dedup and prune rules. How self-standing the authored question can be depends on what a note entry holds, which the sibling question on note entry content decides.

The review pass applies step 4's own conflict test to each note: both entries cannot hold as written, while an entry that only refines, narrows, or extends the other is no conflict. It also applies the recorded-state cleanup (the pair is already flagged, or an entry has since been rewritten). A note that passes becomes one block and is deleted. A note the pass judges plainly a refinement, or already covered, is deleted with no block. Doubt resolves toward authoring the block, so a note is dropped only when the refinement verdict is clear. Notes and step 4's own scan share one conflict test, so the set of conflict questions is the same whichever runner noticed the pair first. A false positive from an answer skill's analyse step costs nothing downstream: no alternatives, recommendation, or answer cycle, and no hold on `/derive-tasks`. The review pass now deletes a recorded conflict on its own judgment, with no block and no answer, which moves it past the tidy side's 'remove only what recorded state covers' line. A wrong refinement verdict loses a real conflict silently: only the `Requirements-review:` commit diff shows the deleted note, and the pair then reaches `/derive-tasks`, where only the tie-break rule settles it.

The review pass applies step 4's conflict test and the recorded-state cleanup to each note, as in the re-testing option. A note it confirms becomes one block and is deleted, and a note already covered by recorded state (pair already flagged, or an entry rewritten) is deleted with no block. A note it judges a refinement is neither authored nor deleted: it stays under `## Noted contradictions` and is named in the pass's report as a git-absent advisory, so the user can delete it by hand or have it authored. The next pass sees it again. It keeps the pass's 'when in doubt, flag rather than delete' rule. A note the pass disagrees with is never thrown away on the pass's judgment alone, yet it does not cost a question cycle or hold task derivation, because a kept note does not affect `list`'s convergence verdict. A third state appears, a note that is neither a question nor resolved. It can stay through convergence and task derivation, so `/derive-tasks`' tie-break and the handling of leftover notes at finish (the sibling question on leftover notes) must cover it. Every later pass re-tests it and repeats the advisory, and nothing in the workflow ever settles it unless the user acts.

open-question.question: Does the `/derive-tasks` tie-break rule apply only to the pairs listed under `## Noted contradictions`, or to any two `## Decisions` entries the runner finds cannot both hold while deriving the briefs?
open-question.recommendation: It matches the goal's wording and the field record, where every pair that reached task derivation was unnoted, recorded by the sweep or by hand; noted pairs are taken as noted with no re-judging, and a brief that cannot satisfy both entries already forces the runner to notice the pair, so the rule only states what then governs.
open-question.alternative: The tie-break rule covers every pair of `## Decisions` entries that cannot both hold. Every pair listed under `## Noted contradictions` is taken as conflicting as noted, without re-judging. Any other pair the runner itself finds conflicting while building the briefs and the coverage matrix is resolved the same way, and the later-recorded entry governs. Nothing is flagged for either kind. It matches the goal's wording ("where two decisions cannot both hold") and closes the gap the field record shows: sweep-recorded and hand-edited conflicts that reach `/derive-tasks` get the same stated rule as noted ones, not an arbitrary silent winner. `/derive-tasks` now forms a contradiction judgment over the unnoted entries. A runner that wrongly reads a refinement as a conflict silently drops the earlier entry's content from the briefs, with no flag to catch it. The rule also needs a way to tell which entry was recorded later that works when no note exists, an axis the later-entry-determination sibling owns.

The tie-break rule covers exactly the pairs listed under `## Noted contradictions`. Each listed pair is taken as conflicting as noted, with no re-judging, and its later-recorded entry governs the brief. For any other pair of `## Decisions` entries, `/derive-tasks` states no rule: it gains no step that reads entries against each other, and a conflict the runner happens to notice is left to its own discretion, as today. Nothing is flagged either way. The rule stays mechanical and bounded. It fires only on pairs a single-question answer skill already judged at fold time, so `/derive-tasks` takes on no new contradiction judgment, which mirrors the sweep forming none. It also keeps the review pass's consistency step as the one place an unnoted conflict is noticed. It does not cover the case the field record shows reaching task derivation: pairs no note recorded, from the sweep (which writes no notes) or from a hand edit. Those still get the silent, rule-less winner seen in `milestone_43`. Its usefulness also depends on a note naming the pair clearly enough for the runner to find both entries, an axis the note-content sibling owns.

The tie-break rule covers only the pairs listed under `## Noted contradictions`, but the runner re-checks each one against the two entries as written and applies the rule only where it confirms they cannot both hold. A noted pair it judges compatible, for example a refinement, has both entries covered as requirements. For unnoted pairs there is no rule, and the runner's discretion applies as today. Nothing is flagged. A note recorded in error or made stale never causes a still-valid earlier constraint to be dropped from the briefs, and the scope stays bounded to pairs someone already suspected. It adds a contradiction judgment to `/derive-tasks` while still leaving unnoted conflicts without a rule, so it carries the costs of both narrow and broad scope and the full benefit of neither. A pair re-judged as compatible is also dropped without any trace, since nothing is flagged.

The tie-break rule covers every pair of `## Decisions` entries the runner itself judges cannot both hold, and notes and unnoted pairs are treated alike.
